The summary of Block Diffusion RooflinesPrevious: IntroductionNext: 1 · Setup

The later chapters derive the gain \(\Gamma\) of block text diffusion (TD) over autoregressive decoding (AR) one result at a time. This chapter states the results first, so that each chapter can be read as the proof of one of them: the headline numbers, a quiz, four takeaways, the symbols, the quantities that move \(\Gamma\), the three regimes that occur in practice, and what the roofline model leaves out.

Before reading on

Which decoder does the roofline model make faster?

Six settings of model, accelerator, batch and context. For each, decide whether block text diffusion (TD) or autoregressive decoding (AR) has the higher throughput under the roofline model. Each answer comes with the roofline that decides it, and the rest of the book explains why.

\[ \Gamma \;=\; \frac{1}{\omega}\cdot\frac{\min\bigl(\class{mj-td}{I_{TD}},\,I^\star\bigr)}{\min\bigl(\class{mj-ar}{I_{AR}},\,I^\star\bigr)},\qquad \omega = S\,r + 1 \]

Proposition 1, the result of Part 2, with the symbols defined in the table below.

In the equations, AR quantities are in blue and TD quantities in orange, as in the figures. Select any formula to see what its symbols mean.

How the numbers are counted

Every gain in Parts 1–7 is a ratio of roofline bounds, counted in one of three ways.

A roofline time is a lower bound on the time of a pass, so each throughput is an upper bound, and \(\Gamma\) is the ratio of two such bounds, not a measurement. Part 11 compares these bounds with throughput measured in vLLM. The three accountings below differ in what they include, and each number in the book says which one it uses. For DiffusionGemma on an H200:

In the interactive figures and the cards, the intensities \(\class{mj-ar}{I_{AR}}\) and \(\class{mj-td}{I_{TD}}\) are those of Definition 3, without the vocabulary, except in the intensity tabs of Figure 19 and the calculator's maps, which use the exact accounting of the appendix; next to an exact gain, the regime of a pass is given instead as the share of the peak compute that it uses. The cards quote the closed-form values of the propositions, at zero context where Part 3 does, unless a readout says exact. A fourth variant, the kernel-by-kernel timing rule of Part 5, can be switched on in Figure 9 and in the calculator.

Four things to remember
  1. TD trades work for reuse. A canvas of \(b\) tokens costs \(\omega\) forward passes instead of one, so TD does \(\omega\) times more FLOPs per token than AR. In return, every byte it reads from memory serves \(b\) positions instead of one. Try it in Figure 4
  2. The best batch is the one at which a TD pass just becomes compute-bound. At smaller batches TD is still memory-bound, and the gain grows as a larger batch lowers the linear penalty. At larger batches TD already runs at peak while AR keeps speeding up, so the gain falls, inversely proportional to \(B\) at short context once AR touches every expert. Try it in Figure 9
  3. At long context the batch stops mattering. Both decoders are then reading the KV cache, which belongs to one sequence, so no batch can share it. What still separates them is when they become compute-bound: an AR step reads the cache for one query and never reaches the ridge, while a TD pass reads it once for \(b\) queries and does. Try it in Figure 13
  4. A higher ridge point means more to gain. Whenever TD is compute-bound and AR is not, the gain scales with \(I^\star\), because \(I^\star\) measures the compute AR leaves idle. However, TD then needs more to reach the ridge: a larger batch at short context, and a canvas longer than \(I^\star/I_{\mathrm{attn}}\) at long context. On a DGX Spark, 273 GB/s against the 7.9 GB that an AR step of DiffusionGemma reads per token in BF16 (batch 1, context 1k, vocabulary included) caps AR at about 35 tokens per second and 0.2% of the chip's BF16 compute; the remaining 99.8% of the compute is available to TD. Try it in Figure 16

What drives the gain

Canvas cost, \(\omega\)

A canvas costs \(\omega = Sr+1\) forward passes. This divides the gain in every regime.

\[ \begin{gathered} \omega = S\,r + 1,\\[4pt] \Gamma = \frac{1}{\omega}\cdot\frac{\min(\class{mj-td}{I_{TD}},\,I^\star)}{\min(\class{mj-ar}{I_{AR}},\,I^\star)}. \end{gathered} \]

\(S\) denoising passes, each costing \(r\) forward passes (\(r \lt 1\) for a smaller denoiser), and one commit pass that writes the canvas to the KV cache. The intensity of a pass does not depend on \(S\), so under Proposition 1 the gain is exactly proportional to \(1/\omega\): halving \(S\) from 14 to 7 takes \(\omega\) from 15 to 8 and multiplies \(\Gamma\) by \(15/8\) in every regime, whatever it costs in quality.

Proposition 1 · Figure 4

Canvas length, \(b\)

Every byte a TD pass reads serves \(b\) positions. While TD is memory-bound this sets the gain, through \(\mathrm{TPF} = b/\omega\). It also sets the batch at which TD becomes compute-bound, which scales like \(1/b\).

\[ \begin{gathered} \mathrm{TPF} = \frac{b}{\omega},\qquad \class{mj-td}{I_{TD}} = \frac{b}{\Pi}\,\class{mj-ar}{I_{AR}},\\[4pt] \class{mj-td}{B^\star_{TD}} \approx \frac{I^\star s_w\class{mj-td}{W_{TD}}}{2b\,N_{\mathrm{act}}}. \end{gathered} \]

While a TD pass is memory-bound, \(\Gamma = \mathrm{TPF}/\Pi\) grows with \(b\). Once it is compute-bound, \(\Gamma = I^\star/(\omega \class{mj-ar}{I_{AR}})\) no longer depends on \(b\): a longer canvas reaches that regime at a smaller batch, and so raises the best gain, which over integer batches sits at the last memory-bound batch or the first compute-bound one.

The gain when the linear layers dominate · Figure 9

Linear penalty, \(\Pi_{\mathrm{lin}}\)

A canvas of 256 positions routes to almost every expert, while an AR step at batch \(B\) reaches about \(kB\) while \(kB \ll E\). At batch 1 the penalty is close to total over active parameters (7.9 for DiffusionGemma); it falls to 1 as the batch grows.

\[ \begin{gathered} \Pi_{\mathrm{lin}}(B) = \frac{\class{mj-td}{W_{TD}}(B)}{\class{mj-ar}{W_{AR}}(B)},\\[4pt] \class{mj-ar}{W_{AR}}(B) = W_{\mathrm{ne}} + L\,U_{E,k}(B)\,W^e,\\[2pt] \class{mj-td}{W_{TD}}(B) = W_{\mathrm{ne}} + L\,U_{E,k}(Bb)\,W^e,\\[4pt] U_{E,k}(N) = E\Bigl[1 - \bigl(1 - \tfrac{k}{E}\bigr)^{N}\Bigr]. \end{gathered} \]

\(U_{E,k}(N)\) is the expected number of distinct experts that \(N\) positions touch in one layer. A canvas routes \(Bb\) positions and touches almost all \(E = 128\); an AR step routes \(B\) and touches about \(kB\) while \(kB \ll E\), with \(k = 8\). The dense part \(W_{\mathrm{ne}} = 1.66\)B is read by both and dilutes the ratio from \(E/k = 16\) to 7.9. Dense models have \(\Pi_{\mathrm{lin}} = 1\).

Proposition 3 · Definition 4

Attention penalty, \(\Pi_{\mathrm{attn}}\)

The attention penalty is 1 for dense and windowed attention, since the canvas reads the cache once for \(b\) queries. It exceeds 1 for sparse attention, where each query selects its own tokens and the canvas reads the union. With a free scan it is the selection penalty \(\Pi_{\mathrm{sel}}\), which has the formula of the expert penalty \(\Pi_E\), with the canvas length in the role of the batch size.

\[ \begin{gathered} \Pi_{\mathrm{attn}}(C) - 1 = \frac{\nu_S\,\bigl[\,U_{C,m}(b) - m\,\bigr]}{\class{mj-ar}{Q^{AR}_{\mathrm{attn}}}(C)},\\[4pt] U_{C,m}(b) = C\Bigl[1 - \bigl(1 - \tfrac{m}{C}\bigr)^{b}\Bigr] \quad (C \ge m). \end{gathered} \]

Only sparse layers contribute: each query selects its own \(m\) cached tokens, and the canvas reads the union, \(U_{C,m}(b)\) tokens, up to \(\min(bm, C)\). This is the expert penalty \(\Pi_E\) again, with cached tokens in the role of experts and the canvas length in the role of the batch. It is 1 while \(C \le m\), largest for \(m \lt C \lesssim bm\), and returns to 1 as \(C \to \infty\), when the union stops growing and the indexer's scan carries the bytes.

Proposition 5 · sparse attention

Batch, \(B\)

The weights are shared by the whole batch, so a larger batch raises AR's intensity. It helps TD first, by shrinking \(\Pi_{\mathrm{lin}}\), and AR after that. It does nothing for the cache, which is per sequence.

\[ Q^{X}(B, C) = \underbrace{\frac{s_wW_X(B)}{B}}_{\text{weights}} + \underbrace{Q^{X}_{\mathrm{attn}}(C)}_{\text{cache}}. \]

For \(X \in \{AR, TD\}\), the weights are shared by the batch and each sequence brings its own cache. A larger batch divides the weight bytes per sequence and leaves the cache bytes unchanged, so it raises both intensities at short context. At first it helps TD more, because \(\Pi_{\mathrm{lin}}\) falls; once a TD pass is compute-bound it only raises \(\class{mj-ar}{I_{AR}}\), and \(\Gamma = I^\star/(\omega \class{mj-ar}{I_{AR}})\) falls, down to parity near batch 109 (Proposition 1 at zero context; 118 in the exact accounting over a whole generation).

Proposition 4 · Figure 9

Context, \(C\)

As the context grows, attention bytes overtake the weights, and the intensities move from their linear values to their attention values: with dense global layers \(\class{mj-ar}{I_{AR}} \to I_{\mathrm{attn}}\) and \(\class{mj-td}{I_{TD}} \to b\,I_{\mathrm{attn}}\), and with sparse global layers \(\class{mj-ar}{I_{AR}} \to I_{\mathrm{idx}}\) (Proposition 6).

\[ \begin{gathered} I_X = \theta^X_{\mathrm{lin}}\,I^X_{\mathrm{lin}} + \theta^X_{\mathrm{attn}}\,I^X_{\mathrm{attn}},\\[4pt] \theta^X_{\mathrm{attn}} = \frac{Q^X_{\mathrm{attn}}}{Q^X}. \end{gathered} \]

Each intensity is the byte-weighted average of its two parts (Proposition 2). As \(C\) grows, the cache's share \(\theta^X_{\mathrm{attn}}\) goes to 1 and the intensities go to their attention values: \(\class{mj-ar}{I_{AR}} \to I_{\mathrm{attn}} = 8\) on DiffusionGemma's global layers, far below every ridge, and \(\class{mj-td}{I_{TD}} \to b\,I_{\mathrm{attn}} = 2{,}048\), above every ridge in this book.

Proposition 2 · Figure 13

The three regimes that occur

AR compute-bound
\(\Gamma = 1/\omega\)

TD is then compute-bound as well. Both run at peak, and TD does \(\omega\) times the work. This regime is rare for MoE decoding: DiffusionGemma on an H200 would need a batch of about 1,600 at zero context, and no batch suffices beyond about 135 tokens of context, where AR's FLOPs per sequence grow more slowly with \(C\) than \(I^\star\) times its cache bytes.

Both passes run at the peak, so time is FLOPs, and a canvas spends \(\omega\) times AR's FLOPs per token: \(\Gamma \le 1/\omega\), equal to it under Proposition 1. AR reaches the ridge at

\[ \begin{gathered} \class{mj-ar}{B^\star_{AR}} = \frac{I^\star s_wW_{\mathrm{tot}}}{2N_{\mathrm{act}}}\\[4pt] = \frac{206 \times 2 \times 24.5\text{B}}{2 \times 3.08\text{B}} \approx 1{,}640. \end{gathered} \]

This closed form takes zero context. By Proposition 8, beyond about 135 tokens of context no batch makes an AR step compute-bound. In addition, holding 1,640 sequences of 9k tokens, the 1k prompt and 8k generated tokens of the running example, would take about 650 GB of KV cache, more than four H200s hold.

Corollary 1 · Proposition 8

Both memory-bound
\(\Gamma = \mathrm{TPF}/\Pi\)

TD's extra FLOPs add no time. Each read serves TPF tokens, divided by the penalty of whichever bytes dominate: 17.07 / 7.94 ≈ 2.15 at batch 1.

Time is bytes. Per sequence, an AR step reads \(\class{mj-ar}{Q^{AR}}\) for one token; a canvas reads \(\omega\) times \(\class{mj-td}{Q^{TD}} = \Pi\,\class{mj-ar}{Q^{AR}}\) for \(b\) tokens. Hence

\[ \Gamma = \frac{\class{mj-ar}{Q^{AR}}}{\omega\,\Pi\,\class{mj-ar}{Q^{AR}}/b} = \frac{\mathrm{TPF}}{\Pi}. \]

TD's extra FLOPs are hidden under the memory time. At batch 1, \(\mathrm{TPF} = 256/15 = 17.07\) and \(\Pi \approx \Pi_{\mathrm{lin}}(1) = 7.94\), so \(\Gamma \approx 2.15\); the exact accounting at a fixed context of 1k gives 2.53, and 2.55 over the whole generation.

Corollary 1 · Figure 4

AR memory-, TD compute-bound
\(\Gamma = \dfrac{I^\star}{\omega\,\class{mj-ar}{I_{AR}}}\)

TD uses the compute that AR leaves idle. At short context this falls with the batch, inversely proportional to \(B\) once AR touches every expert; at long context it tends to \(I^\star/(\omega I_{\mathrm{attn}})\), 1.72 on an H200, at any batch.

TD runs at the peak \(\pi\) and AR at \(\class{mj-ar}{I_{AR}}\,\beta\), so TD's FLOPs run \(I^\star/\class{mj-ar}{I_{AR}}\) times faster and it does \(\omega\) times as many. The gain is the compute that AR leaves idle, divided by TD's extra work. At short context \(\class{mj-ar}{I_{AR}}\) grows with the batch and \(\Gamma\) reaches 1 near batch 109. At long context \(\class{mj-ar}{I_{AR}} \to I_{\mathrm{attn}}\), and at any batch

\[ \Gamma \to \frac{I^\star}{\omega\,I_{\mathrm{attn}}} = \frac{206}{15 \times 8} = 1.72. \]

Proposition 7 · Figure 16

While AR is memory-bound, \(\Gamma = \min\bigl(\mathrm{TPF}/\Pi,\ I^\star/(\omega \class{mj-ar}{I_{AR}})\bigr)\). The first term grows with the batch and the second shrinks, which is why the best batch is where TD turns compute-bound.

What the formulas leave out

  • Vocabulary and self-conditioning. With self-conditioning, each denoising pass feeds the token distribution predicted by the previous pass back in through the embedding matrix. Per token, TD runs \(2S-1\) vocabulary-sized matrix multiplications against AR's one, and a smaller decoder does not shrink them. The maps and the calculator include them.
  • Timing kernel by kernel. Assumption (A1) times a pass as one kernel in which all of its compute and memory traffic overlap. Timing it kernel by kernel instead moves DiffusionGemma's best batch on an H200 from 5 to 9 (Remark 2, Part 5); the calculator offers both rules.
  • Small effects. The formulas leave out activations (they stay in the processor's caches when consecutive operations are merged into one kernel), KV writes, and the at most \(b\) keys inside the canvas.
  • Keys equal to values on the global layers. DiffusionGemma's global layers project one tensor that serves as both key and value. The book, like vLLM and the kernel of Part 10, caches it twice (\(\kappa^c = 2\)); a cache that stored it once would halve the global layers' bytes, double \(I_{\mathrm{attn}}\) to 16 and halve the long-context limit \(I^\star/(\omega I_{\mathrm{attn}})\) (regime R6, Part 5) from 1.72 to 0.86.
  • Cross-layer KV sharing. It divides the KV cache's size, not the bytes read per pass, since each layer still reads the shared cache. It changes the largest batch that fits in memory, not any intensity.
  • Beyond the roofline. Kernel efficiency, uneven and correlated expert routing (Parts 8–11 measure both on an H200: at batch 8 and above TD runs at 0.46–0.61 of its empirical roofline and AR at 0.43–0.73, and a canvas touches far fewer experts than independent routing predicts), adaptive step counts, correlated token selections, the wait for the first canvas, and quality per step.
